DOWN THE DRAIN -- public money lost

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Billions of Rands lost to corruption, maladministration, misappropriation and fruitless expenditure...how much money exactly has the taxpayer lost due to inadequate oversight? And who's responsible?

Unique Selling Point:
Amid weekly headlines screaming of misappropriation and waste, we pull back to take in the big picture and ask if it's possible to quantify the losses to the South African taxpayer if one adds up the reported losses since 2014, when President Jacob Zuma started his last term.

It's been stated as fact and used in opposition discourse that R700-million has been lost to the fiscus since 1994, due to corruption.

But is it really possible to put a figure to the losses? How can we separate corruption from maladministration, misappropriation or even money lost to law-suits against government departments?

All of these represent resources lost that could have changed South Africans' lives, so we rope in the experts and relevant state departments to help us determine where the greatest losses have been in the last few years and why.

And who are the recurring culprits every year?

We also ask if there is ultimately anyone who can stop the floods of public money going down the drain and present the institutions that we can look to for correction.

Press Release:


Down The Drain
Corruption, wastage and mismanagement at State-owned enterprises and in government departments – that’s the recipe costing South African taxpayers billions of rands
every year. But how much is really going down the drain? Carte Blanche tallies up the costs and the massive losses to State coffers.

Script:


R83-billion to bail out Eskom; R2.3-billion to keep SAA airborne; R1-billion gone at the SABC last year. Prasa probed for alleged corruption of R7.5-billion. South Africans are punch-drunk but the hits just keep coming.

WILLIAM GUMEDE, DIRECTOR: PROGRAMME FOR THE MANAGEMENT OF PUBLIC ENTERPRISES, WITS: It’s almost like monopoly money...you are ordinary person in a shack, I mean you hear billions lost during the year!

LINK: The numbers are so big, it’s beyond our grasp. But it is still our money and when it’s lost, we can’t pay for basics.

Professor William Gumede helped establish the Programme for the Management of Public Enterprises at Wits University.

WILLIAM GUMEDE, DIRECTOR: PROGRAMME FOR THE MANAGEMENT OF PUBLIC ENTERPRISES, WITS: If you take from 1994 up to now and we just used the money that has been wasted through corruption and money that’s been lost to irregular expenditure, the state won’t need any money from anywhere.

Axed as finance minister but still a member of parliament, Pravin Gordhan uses every speaking invitation to help people connect the dots between state money lost and risks to economic growth.

(Univ. of Johannesburg, 26 July 2017) PRAVIN GORDHAN: Now is the time to make a decision on where you stand. If we keep quiet we’re going to slump into a ten year disaster.

PRAVIN GORDHAN, FORMER FINANCE MINISTER: People stop us in very different places in this country, all of whom understand that corruption is bad for South Africa. And they also know who are the principal parties that are involved and they understand that South Africa needs change. They want to actually see leaders who are spending most of their time serving South Africans rather than serving themselves.

It’s hard to pin-point how much money is really lost every year. Auditor-General Kimi Makwetu is tasked by the Constitution to ensure the state spends wisely.

KIMI MAKWETU, AUDITOR-GENERAL: If it’s in education we want to see where is that building that you said you you’re going to build to add the classes.

DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Where’s the slips?

KIMI MAKWETU, AUDITOR-GENERAL: Where’s the slips? Which account did you put that money into so that we can trace it? Where’s the invoice? You don’t have it. No, that sounds like it’s irregular.

Government comprises over 400 entities from municipalities to provincial and national departments. In his latest reports, the AG found that nearly R80-billion rands was not properly accounted for.

KIMI MAKWETU, AUDITOR-GENERAL: So we are sounding a warning, if you like, to the people who are charged with governance in the system to say, if you do not take steps now to investigate the circumstances that lead to finances being handled in such a manner, before you know it, you will find that you are paying for things you never received.

DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Can you help us crunch the numbers? South African tax-payer money that’s been lost in terms of corruption and mismanagement, how do we put a figure to it?

PRAVIN GORDHAN, FORMER FINANCE MINISTER: There’s several techniques. The first is the Auditor General’s numbers. The second example would be to actually to do a dipstick test on big tenders and not so big tenders, because there has been a pattern in our country where there’s extra invoicing of amounts. And the third is called the tax gap. And the tax gap is the difference between the tax that you should be collecting and the tax that you actually collect.

On Gordhan’s advice, we calculated that easily R65-billion but possibly more than R200-billion were lost last year. This worst case scenario equals a fifth of all the tax collected -- that’s nearly R30 000 per taxpayer gone. Economist Mike Schüssler says corruption is complex.

MIKE SCHÜSSLER, ECONOMIST: So the state of corruption isn’t only about the things that we pay, but the services that are delivered to us or that are not delivered to us...add all of that up, it is far over 200-billion a year...nobody has got the exact number and yes it’s very difficult because corruption is what it is. It’s secretive, it is quiet, it tries to stay hidden and it’s very difficult to uncover it.

DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: What will 200 billion buy us per year?

MIKE SCHÜSSLER, ECONOMIST: We could more than double the welfare grants to people; we could probably lower the tax rates; and that would get the economy growing...

PRAVIN GORDHAN, FORMER FINANCE MINISTER: More doctors could be deployed...or you could contribute that to university fees for example.

Let’s take R200-billion a year. That would build 5882 schools or 900 000 fifty square meter houses. It would pay about 1.2-million primary school teachers’ salaries or the university fees for 6.6-million students, for a year.

DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Can the economy survive this? These losses?

PRAVIN GORDHAN, FORMER FINANCE MINISTER: Well, the economy can survive anything.

DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: We’ve seen that.

PRAVIN GORDHAN, FORMER FINANCE MINISTER: It depends on ultimately what do you mean by survival. I mean there’s bare survival as supposed to doing better and well...

DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: So who are the culprits here?

MIKE SCHÜSSLER, ECONOMIST: State owned enterprises…government on both the national and the provincial level and we mustn’t only think corruption comes from one family. I don’t see for example with…a social security and social grants issues that we have. I don’t see the name of the Guptas there. I think we don’t understand how big this thing is.

We have over 700 state-owned enterprises, many apartheid era relics. As chairperson of Parliament’s Standing Committee on Public Accounts or Scopa, Themba Godi has seen the rot spread over twelve years.

THEMBA GODI, CHAIRPERSON, SCOPA: The larger problem is with the state owned companies and what we found is that where private audit firms audit, their disclosure of information is very weak. With the SABC it was only when the Auditor General took over that a lot of these irregular expenditure, right now we are talking R5 billion and counting of irregular expenditure over years, only then did those things come out.

LINK: Municipalities and state-owned entities like the SABC, Eskom, Prasa and the SAA are some of the main culprits when it comes to money going astray. But the buck must stop somewhere.

DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: How does it make you feel when you come across overt examples of people who don’t care about where the money goes?

KIMI MAKWETU, AUDITOR-GENERAL: It springs up a message that says that those people do not just have little care for the money. They also do not care for the people who are on the receiving end of what that money was meant to achieve.

At municipal level where state money is used for everyday services, the rising tide of violent protest against a lack of service delivery reveals the growing discontent at state losses.

THEMBA GODI, CHAIRPERSON, SCOPA: It is a very painful thing for me having committed a good part of my life in the fight for freedom motivated by nothing but to see the lives of our people improve...you can have good legislation but if you don’t have the people with the right mindset they remain nothing but statements on paper.

PRAVIN GORDHAN, FORMER FINANCE MINISTER: Sometimes it’s small things that actually drive people into the wrong kind of habits. You know you start using a state facility for your personal use when you shouldn’t be doing it and then you get a loan or something from somebody and that then begins to compromise your integrity and then you decide that you want to become more greedy and worse is reckless greed. Reckless greed is where you say I want accumulate as much money as I can or to manipulate as many people and entities as I can and I don’t care what happens to the country.

WILLIAM GUMEDE, DIRECTOR: PROGRAMME FOR THE MANAGEMENT OF PUBLIC ENTERPRISES, WITS: I think it happened gradually, but it accelerated when Jacob Zuma became president of the country. People have assumed from day one when we created this new democracy, that the leaders in government is always going to be good. The biggest weakness of the Constitution now is that it gives too much power to the president. Parliament will have to hold government accountable.
Scopa and the AG are now fighting to strengthen the sticks that the watchdogs of democracy can wield. Until now they could only question and chastise.

THEMBA GODI, CHAIRPERSON, SCOPA: We have now taken it a step further. We have sought to involve the law enforcement agencies so that in instances where we find criminality, we do not wait anymore for the officials to open cases. But we want to refer it ourselves so that people could know that for wrongdoing there will be consequences.

The AG is asking parliament for the power to claim the money back from officials themselves if government paid more for goods or services than the market price.

KIMI MAKWETU, AUDITOR-GENERAL: The difference between the price that you ought to have picked from the database of National Treasury and the price that you decided to go and commit government to is yours, it’s for your own account.

LINK: Seemingly paralysed by the sheer scale of the financial problems facing our country, is there anything you and I can actually do?

WILLIAM GUMEDE, DIRECTOR: PROGRAMME FOR THE MANAGEMENT OF PUBLIC ENTERPRISES, WITS: Keep the pressure on...the only way really to do it, is to vote...not to vote for the ANC. That's the only way the party, I am afraid and the leaders are going to listen...

DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: What happens if we don’t fix this fast?

MIKE SCHÜSSLER, ECONOMIST: It is probably going to have to lead to many people going to jail...if we don’t do it, the costs to our economy is going to become unbearable at some stage and at that stage, the majority of taxpayers will find ways not to pay taxes or to leave the country and then...

DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: A tax revolt?

MIKE SCHÜSSLER, ECONOMIST: A tax revolt.

PRAVIN GORDHAN, FORMER FINANCE MINISTER: We must all speak up when things are wrong. But equally compliment people when they do the right things as well. So not everything is wrong. Otherwise we will be a totally failed state and we’re not. You need the principles as your beacon...if your eye is on what kind of South Africa we want, then that is something that all of us continue to strive for.

PRAVIN GORDHAN, FORMER FINANCE MINISTER: Sometimes it’s small things that actually drive people into the wrong kind of habits. You know you start using a state facility for your personal use when you shouldn’t be doing it and then you get a loan or something from somebody and that then begins to compromise your integrity and then you decide that you want to become more greedy and worse is reckless greed. Reckless greed is where you say I want accumulate as much money as I can or to manipulate as many people and entities as I can and I don’t care what happens to the country. WILLIAM GUMEDE, DIRECTOR: PROGRAMME FOR THE MANAGEMENT OF PUBLIC ENTERPRISES, WITS: I think it happened gradually, but it accelerated when Jacob Zuma became president of the country. People have assumed from day one when we created this new democracy, that the leaders in government is always going to be good. The biggest weakness of the Constitution now is that it gives too much power to the president. Parliament will have to hold government accountable. Scopa and the AG are now fighting to strengthen the sticks that the watchdogs of democracy can wield. Until now they could only question and chastise. THEMBA GODI, CHAIRPERSON, SCOPA: We have now taken it a step further. We have sought to involve the law enforcement agencies so that in instances where we find criminality, we do not wait anymore for the officials to open cases. But we want to refer it ourselves so that people could know that for wrongdoing there will be consequences. The AG is asking parliament for the power to claim the money back from officials themselves if government paid more for goods or services than the market price. KIMI MAKWETU, AUDITOR-GENERAL: The difference between the price that you ought to have picked from the database of National Treasury and the price that you decided to go and commit government to is yours, it’s for your own account. LINK: Seemingly paralysed by the sheer scale of the financial problems facing our country, is there anything you and I can actually do? WILLIAM GUMEDE, DIRECTOR: PROGRAMME FOR THE MANAGEMENT OF PUBLIC ENTERPRISES, WITS: Keep the pressure on...the only way really to do it, is to vote...not to vote for the ANC. That's the only way the party, I am afraid and the leaders are going to listen... DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: What happens if we don’t fix this fast? MIKE SCHÜSSLER, ECONOMIST: It is probably going to have to lead to many people going to jail...if we don’t do it, the costs to our economy is going to become unbearable at some stage and at that stage, the majority of taxpayers will find ways not to pay taxes or to leave the country and then... DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: A tax revolt? MIKE SCHÜSSLER, ECONOMIST: A tax revolt. PRAVIN GORDHAN, FORMER FINANCE MINISTER: We must all speak up when things are wrong. But equally compliment people when they do the right things as well. So not everything is wrong. Otherwise we will be a totally failed state and we’re not. You need the principles as your beacon...if your eye is on what kind of South Africa we want, then that is something that all of us continue to strive for.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Billions of Rands lost to corruption, maladministration, misappropriation and fruitless expenditure...how much money exactly has the taxpayer lost due to inadequate oversight? And who's responsible?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Amid weekly headlines screaming of misappropriation and waste, we pull back to take in the big picture and ask if it's possible to quantify the losses to the South African taxpayer if one adds up the reported losses since 2014, when President Jacob Zuma started his last term. It's been stated as fact and used in opposition discourse that R700-million has been lost to the fiscus since 1994, due to corruption. But is it really possible to put a figure to the losses? How can we separate corruption from maladministration, misappropriation or even money lost to law-suits against government departments? All of these represent resources lost that could have changed South Africans' lives, so we rope in the experts and relevant state departments to help us determine where the greatest losses have been in the last few years and why. And who are the recurring culprits every year? We also ask if there is ultimately anyone who can stop the floods of public money going down the drain and present the institutions that we can look to for correction.
